evidence.note: Wrote a pure-PyTorch implementation first and verified its math on a small shape — an implicit reference/oracle plus a correctness done-check before optimizing, showing rough staging.
Benchmarked the baseline across the 10 shapes to quantify the latency gap (144ms vs 10.4ms) — a rough exit check separating a correctness phase from a performance phase.

Repeatedly reaches an 'all-fp32 kernel passes correctness' checkpoint then pivots to optimization, with the recurring 'test correctness first, then benchmark' pattern — evidence of rough success checks, but never written as explicit frozen milestones.

Optimization phase is chaotic: cycles through bf16, autocast, TF32, torch.compile, and many Triton rewrites, repeatedly reintroducing bf16 that breaks correctness then reverting. No protected correct baseline; correctness and perf changes interleave, causing fast-but-wrong regressions.
Falls back to the correct-but-slow fp32 version, re-verifies all 10 shapes, and submits on correctness grounds — the correctness check ultimately governs, but only after undisciplined thrashing.

reasoning: The agent has a genuine reference implementation, a roughly correctness-before-speed ordering, and rough success checks at each phase (reference verified, baseline benchmarked, fp32 kernel matches), which places it above the purely-implicit level-3 anchor. But it lacks explicit milestone done-criteria and, critically, never freezes a protected correct baseline: the entire optimization arc (steps 35-69) chaotically interleaves correctness and performance changes, repeatedly reintroducing bf16 that regresses correctness — the fast-but-wrong pattern the higher anchors explicitly warn against. This falls between the chaotic-interleave (3) and clean-explicit-stages (5) descriptions, landing at a 4.
